torrid

/TOR-id/ - the stress falls on TOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Torrid means extremely hot.

By two o'clock the plaza is torrid, and the whole town shutters itself until the light begins to slant.

Example

On the old coal liners, the worst berth aboard was three decks below the passengers' dance floor. In the stokehold, men fed the boilers in singlets soaked through in minutes, watched over by an officer whose main duty was the clock: fifteen minutes at the doors, then out, because the air itself was torrid — near fifty degrees — and no amount of willpower changed what that did to a body.

Torrid is the exact word for that space, because it means extremely hot — heat at the top of the scale, heat that punishes. A stuffy cabin is a complaint; a torrid stokehold is a medical schedule. The word carries that violence, which is why geographers gave the equator's belt the name Torrid Zone.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

scorching: Scorching is heat named for what it does — it burns whatever it touches: pavement, paint, the back of your neck. Torrid is heat named for its rank: extreme, punishing, the top of the scale, whether or not anything has burned yet.

blistering: Blistering measures heat on your own skin — sun that raises blisters, a handrail you cannot hold. Torrid measures the place itself: air so extremely hot it punishes everyone in it, the heat that named the equator's whole belt.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

frigid: cold at the same extreme

temperate: mild, in the comfortable middle of the scale

Where it sits · how fierce the heat gets

balmy → sweltering → torrid

balmy vs. torrid: Balmy is warmth as a gift — shirtsleeve evenings, windows open; it is the mildest air on this scale, nowhere near the punishing heat of torrid.

sweltering vs. torrid: Sweltering goes further than balmy — heat you sweat through, heavy and airless; torrid claims the most: heat with violence in it, the kind that names the equator's whole belt of the globe.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — torr-: to scorch, to parch (Latin torrere)

Suffix — -id: in a given state (as in humid, arid)

Put it together: Torr- (to scorch) + -id (in a given state) = in a scorched state. Latin torrere meant to parch with heat, and its family ran two ways: tostus, "scorched," strolled through Old French into English as toast, while torrens — first "boiling, seething," then a seething stream — became torrent. Bread, floods, and heat waves, all from one busy verb.

Use the root in a new word: toast: Toast is torr- at breakfast: bread scorched brown by open heat, from Latin tostus, "scorched."

Root Check

Word Choice

literary / forceful

Torrid is heat with drama: reach for it when hot undersells the danger — torrid noons, the Torrid Zone. Keep it apart from this unit's arid, which measures rainfall rather than temperature: a bayou August is torrid and soaking wet, and a high desert can be arid under frost. Sportswriters borrow the word for a torrid pace or a torrid stretch of scoring — no thermometer involved, all the intensity kept.
